entries.661cebc18079dbc7fc3bce04ebe71b9419e1f15e: <div sID="gen15788" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Isa.14" sID="Isa.14"/> <div eID="gen15788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15789" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15790" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. More weight is added to the burden of Babylon, enough to sink it like a mill-stone; I. It is Israel's cause that is to be pleaded in this quarrel with Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1-Isa.14.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. The king of Babylon, for the time being, shall be remarkably brought down and triumphed over, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4-Isa.14.20">ver. 4-20</reference>. 3. The whole race of the Babylonians shall be cut off and extirpated, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.21-Isa.14.23">ver. 21-23</reference>. II. A confirmation of the prophecy of the destruction of Babylon, which was a thing at a distance, is here given in the prophecy of the destruction of the Assyrian army that invaded the land, which happened not long after, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27">ver. 24-27</reference>. III. The success of Hezekiah against the Philistines is here foretold, and the advantages which his people would gain thereby, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.28-Isa.14.32">ver. 28-32</reference>.
entries.bf23b66c7f0bbdae2fc19d55e190ee20246492db: <div eID="gen15790" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15789" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 739.)</title> <div sID="gen15791" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for servants and handmaids: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors. <hi type="super">3</hi> And it shall come to pass in the day that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve, <div eID="gen15791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15792" type="x-p"/> This comes in here as the reason why Babylon must be overthrown and ruined, because God has mercy in store for his people, and therefore, 1. The injuries done to them must be reckoned for and revenged upon their persecutors. Mercy to Jacob will be wrath and ruin to Jacob's impenitent implacable adversaries, such as Babylon was. 2. The yoke of oppression which Babylon had long laid on their necks must be broken off, and they must be set at liberty; and, in order to this, the destruction of Babylon is as necessary as the destruction of Egypt and Pharaoh was to their deliverance out of that house of bondage. The same prediction is a promise to God's people and a threatening to their enemies, as the same providence has a bright side towards Israel and a black or dark side towards the Egyptians. Observe, <div eID="gen15792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15793" type="x-p"/> I. The ground of these favours to Jacob and Israel—the kindness God had for them and the choice he had made of them (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord will have mercy on Jacob,</hi> the seed of Jacob now captives in Babylon; he will make it to appear that he has compassion on them and has mercy in store for them, and that he will not contend for ever with them, but <hi type="italic">will yet choose them,</hi> will yet again return to them; though he has seemed for a time to refuse and reject them, he will show that they are his chosen people and that the election stands sure." However it may seem to us, God's mercy is not gone, nor does his promise fail, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.8">Ps. lxxvii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen15793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15794" type="x-p"/> II. The particular favours he designed them. 1. He would bring them back to their native soil and air again: The <hi type="italic">Lord will set them in their own land,</hi> out of which they were driven. A settlement in the holy land, the land of promise, is a fruit of God's mercy, distinguishing mercy. 2. Many should be proselyted to their holy religion, and should return with them, induced to do so by the manifest tokens of God's favourable presence with them, the operations of God's grace in them, the operations of God's grace in them, and his providence for them: <hi type="italic">Strangers shall be joined with them,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>. It adds much to the honour and strength of Israel when strangers are joined with them and there are added to the church many from without, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.47">Acts ii. 47</reference>. Let not the church's children be shy of strangers, but receive those whom God receives, and own those who cleave to the house of Jacob. 3. These proselytes should not only be a credit to their cause, but very helpful and serviceable to them in their return home: <hi type="italic">The people</hi> among whom they live <hi type="italic">shall take them,</hi> take care of them, take pity on them, and shall <hi type="italic">bring them to their place</hi>—as friends, loth to part with such good company—as servants, willing to do them all the good offices they could. God's people, wherever their lot is cast, should endeavour thus, by all the instances of an exemplary and winning conversation, to gain an interest in the affections of those about them, and recommend religion to their good opinion. This was fulfilled in the return of the captives from Babylon, when all that were about them, pursuant to Cyrus's proclamation, contributed to their removal (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.4">Ezra i. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.6">6</reference>), not as the Egyptians, because they were sick of them, but because they loved them. 4. They should have the benefit of their service when they had returned home, for many would of choice go with them in the meanest post, rather than not go with them: They <hi type="italic">shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids;</hi> and as the laws of that land saved it from being the purgatory of servants, providing that they should not be oppressed, so the advantages of that land made it the paradise of those servants that had been strangers to the covenants of promise, for there was <hi type="italic">one law to the stranger and to those that were born in the land.</hi> Those whose lot is cast in the land of the Lord, a land of light, should take care that their servants and handmaids may share in the benefit of it, who will then find it better to be possessed in the Lord's land than possessors in any other. 5. They should triumph over their enemies, and those that would not be reconciled to them should be reduced and humbled by them: <hi type="italic">They shall take those captives whose captives they were and shall rule over their oppressors,</hi> righteously, but not revengefully. The Jews perhaps bought Babylonian prisoners out of the hands of the Medes and Persians and made slaves of them. Or this might have its accomplishment in their victories over their enemies in the times of the Maccabees. It is applicable to the success of the gospel (when those were brought into obedience to it who had made the greatest opposition to it, as Paul) and to the interest believers have in Christ's victories over their spiritual enemies, when he led captivity captive, to the power they gain over their own corruptions, and to the dominion the upright shall have in the morning, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>. 6. They should see a happy termination of all their grievances (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall give thee rest from thy sorrow and thy fear, and from thy hard bondage.</hi> God himself undertakes to work a blessed change, (1.) In their state. They shall have rest from their bondage; the days of their affliction, though many, shall have an end; and the rod of the wicked, though it lie long, shall not always lie on their lot. (2.) In their spirit. They shall have rest from their sorrow and fear, sense of their present burdens and dread of worse. Sometimes fear puts the soul into a ferment as much as sorrow does, and those must needs feel themselves very easy to whom God has given rest from both. Those who are freed from the bondage of sin have a foundation laid for true rest from sorrow and fear.
entries.e5dc49d9975e50e0c73a532f880b3cfb68c3f5df: <div eID="gen15794" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of the King of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 739.)</title> <div sID="gen15795" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased! <hi type="super">5</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath broken the staff of the wicked, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the sceptre of the rulers. <hi type="super">6</hi> He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger, is persecuted, <hi type="italic">and</hi> none hindereth. <hi type="super">7</hi> The whole earth is at rest, <hi type="italic">and</hi> is quiet: they break forth into singing. <hi type="super">8</hi> Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the cedars of Lebanon, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us. <hi type="super">9</hi> Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet <hi type="italic">thee</hi> at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. <hi type="super">10</hi> All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us? <hi type="super">11</hi> Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! <hi type="italic">how</hi> art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! <hi type="super">13</hi> For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: <hi type="super">14</hi> I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High. <hi type="super">15</hi> Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit. <hi type="super">16</hi> They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> consider thee, <hi type="italic">saying, Is</hi> this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms; <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> made the world as a wilderness, and destroyed the cities thereof; <hi type="italic">that</hi> opened not the house of his prisoners? <hi type="super">18</hi> All the kings of the nations, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. <hi type="super">19</hi> But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, <hi type="italic">and as</hi> the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou shalt not be joined with them in burial, because thou hast destroyed thy land, <hi type="italic">and</hi> slain thy people: the seed of evildoers shall never be renowned. <hi type="super">21</hi> Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. <hi type="super">22</hi> For I will rise up against them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">23</hi> I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen15795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15796" type="x-p"/> The kings of Babylon, successively, were the great enemies and oppressors of God's people, and therefore the destruction of Babylon, the fall of the king, and the ruin of his family, are here particularly taken notice of and triumphed in. In the day that God has given Israel rest they shall <hi type="italic">take up this proverb against the king of Babylon.</hi> We must not rejoice when our enemy falls, as ours; but when Babylon, the common enemy of God and his Israel, sinks, then <hi type="italic">rejoice over her, thou heaven, and you holy apostles and prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">Rev. xviii. 20</reference>. The Babylonian monarchy bade fair to be an absolute, universal, and perpetual one, and, in these pretensions, vied with the Almighty; it is therefore very justly, not only brought down, but insulted over when it is down; and it is not only the last monarch, Belshazzar, who <hi type="italic">was slain on that night</hi> that Babylon was taken (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Dan. v. 30</reference>), who is here triumphed over, but the whole monarchy, which sunk in him; not without special reference to Nebuchadnezzar, in whom that monarchy was at its height. Now here, <div eID="gen15796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15797" type="x-p"/> I. The fall of the king of Babylon is rejoiced in; and a most curious and elegant composition is here prepared, not to adorn his hearse or monument, but to expose his memory and fix a lasting brand of infamy upon it. It gives us an account of the life and death of this mighty monarch, how he <hi type="italic">went down slain to the pit,</hi> though he had been <hi type="italic">the terror of the mighty in the land of the living,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Ezek. xxxii. 27</reference>. In this parable we may observe, <div eID="gen15797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15798" type="x-p"/> 1. The prodigious height of wealth and power at which this monarch and monarchy arrived. Babylon was a <hi type="italic">golden city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">v. 4</reference> (it is a Chaldee word in the original, which intimates that she used to call herself so), so much did she abound in riches and excel all other cities, as gold does all other metals. She is <hi type="italic">gold-thirsty,</hi> or an exactress of gold (so some read it); for how do men get wealth to themselves but by squeezing it out of others? The New Jerusalem is the only truly golden city, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.18">Rev. xxi. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.21">21</reference>. The king of Babylon, having so much wealth in his dominions and the absolute command of it, by the help of that <hi type="italic">ruled the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">v. 6</reference>), gave them law, read them their doom, and at his pleasure <hi type="italic">weakened the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.12">v. 12</reference>), that they might not be able to make head against him. Such vast and victorious armies did he bring into the field, that, which way soever he looked, he <hi type="italic">made the earth to tremble, and shook kingdoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.16">v. 16</reference>); all his neighbours were afraid of him, and were forced to submit to him. No one man could do this by his own personal strength, but by the numbers he has at his beck. Great tyrants, by making some do what they will, make others suffer what they will. How piteous is the case of mankind, which thus seems to be in a combination against itself, and its own rights and liberties, which could not be ruined but by its own strength! <div eID="gen15798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15799" type="x-p"/> 2. The wretched abuse of all this wealth and power, which the king of Babylon was guilty of, in two instances:— <div eID="gen15799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15800" type="x-p"/> (1.) Great oppression and cruelty. He is known by the name of the <hi type="italic">oppressor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">v. 4</reference>); he has <hi type="italic">the sceptre of the rulers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.5">v. 5</reference>), has the command of all the princes about him; but it is <hi type="italic">the staff of the wicked,</hi> a staff with which he supports himself in his wickedness and wickedly strikes all about him. <hi type="italic">He smote the people,</hi> not in justice, for their correction and reformation, but <hi type="italic">in wrath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">v. 6</reference>), to gratify his own peevish resentments, and that <hi type="italic">with a continual stroke,</hi> pursued them with his forces, and gave them no respite, no breathing time, no cessation of arms. He ruled the nations, but he ruled them <hi type="italic">in anger,</hi> every thing he said and did was in a passion; so that he who had the government of all about him had no government of himself. He <hi type="italic">made the world as a wilderness,</hi> as if he had taken a pride in being the plague of his generation and a curse to mankind, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">v. 17</reference>. Great princes usually glory in building cities, but he gloried in destroying them; see <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">Ps. ix. 6</reference>. Two particular instances, worse than all the rest, are here given of his tyranny:—[1.] That he was severe to his captives (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">v. 17</reference>): He <hi type="italic">opened not the house of his prisoners;</hi> he <hi type="italic">did not let them loose homeward</hi> (so the margin reads it); he kept them in close confinement, and never would suffer any to return to their own land. This refers especially to the people of the Jews, and it is that which fills up the measure of the king of Babylon's iniquity, that he had detained the people of God in captivity and would by no means release them; nay, and by profaning the vessels of God's temple at Jerusalem, did in effect say that they should never return to their former use, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.3">Dan. v. 3</reference>. For this he was quickly and justly turned out by one whose first act was to open the house of God's prisoners and send home the temple vessels. [2.] That he was oppressive to his own subjects (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people;</hi> and what did he get by that, when the wealth of the land and the multitude of the people are the strength and honour of the prince, who never rules so safely, so gloriously, as in the hearts and affections of the people? But tyrants sacrifice their interests to their lusts and passions; and God will reckon with them for their barbarous usage of those who are under their power, whom they think they may use as they please. <div eID="gen15800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15801" type="x-p"/> (2.) Great pride and haughtiness. Notice is here taken of his <hi type="italic">pomp,</hi> the extravagancy of his retinue, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">v. 11</reference>. He affected to appear in the utmost magnificence. But that was not the worst: it was the temper of his mind, and the elevation of that, that ripened him for ruin (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.13-Isa.14.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou has said in thy heart,</hi> like Lucifer, <hi type="italic">I will ascend into heaven.</hi> Here is the language of his vainglory, borrowed perhaps from that of the angels who fell, who not content with their first estate, the post assigned them, would vie with God, and become not only independent of him, but equal with him. Or perhaps it refers to the story of Nebuchadnezzar, who, when he would be more than a man, was justly turned into a brute, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Dan. iv. 30</reference>. The king of Babylon here promises himself, [1.] That in pomp and power he shall surpass all his neighbours, and shall arrive at the very height of earthly glory and felicity, that he shall be as great and happy as this world can make him; that is the heaven of a carnal heart, and to that he hopes to ascend, and to be as far above those about him as the heaven is above the earth. Princes are the stars of God, which give some light to this dark world (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Matt. xxiv. 29</reference>); but he will exalt his throne above them all. [2.] That he shall particularly insult over God's Mount Zion, which Belshazzar, in his last drunken frolic, seems to have had a particular spite against when he called for the vessels of the temple at Jerusalem, to profane them; see <reference osisRef="Dan.5.2">Dan. v. 2</reference>. In the same humour he here said, <hi type="italic">I will sit upon the mount of the congregation</hi> (it is the same word that is used for the holy <hi type="italic">convocations), in the sides of the north;</hi> so Mount Zion is said to be situated, <reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 2</reference>. Perhaps Belshazzar was projecting an expedition to Jerusalem, to triumph in the ruins of it, at the time when God cut him off. [3.] That he shall vie with the God of Israel, of whom he had indeed heard glorious things, that he had his residence <hi type="italic">above the heights of the clouds.</hi> "But thither," says he, "<hi type="italic">will I ascend,</hi> and be as great as he; I will be like him whom they call <hi type="italic">the Most High.</hi>" It is a gracious ambition to covet to be like the Most Holy, for he has said, <hi type="italic">Be you holy, for I am holy;</hi> but it is a sinful ambition to aim to be like the Most High, for he has said, <hi type="italic">He that exalteth himself shall be abased,</hi> and the devil drew our first parents in to eat forbidden fruit by promising them that they should be as gods. [4.] That he shall himself be deified after his death, as some of the first founders of the Assyrian monarchy were, and stars had even their names from them. "But," says he, "<hi type="italic">I will exalt my throne above them</hi> all." Such as this was his pride, which was the undoubted omen of his destruction. <div eID="gen15801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15802" type="x-p"/> 3. The utter ruin that should be brought upon him. It is foretold, (1.) That his wealth and power should be broken, and a final period put to his pomp and pleasure. He has been long an oppressor, but he shall cease to be so, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">v. 4</reference>. Had he ceased to be so by true repentance and reformation, according to the advice Daniel gave to Nebuchadnezzar, it might have been a lengthening of his life and tranquillity. But those that will not cease to sin God will make to cease. "<hi type="italic">The golden city,</hi> which one would have thought might continue for ever, <hi type="italic">has ceased;</hi> there is an end of that Babylon. <hi type="italic">The Lord,</hi> the righteous God, <hi type="italic">has broken the staff of that wicked prince,</hi> broken it over his head, in token of the divesting him of his office. God has taken his power from him, and rendered him incapable of doing any more mischief: he has broken the sceptres; for even these are brittle things, soon broken and often justly." (2.) That he himself should be seized: <hi type="italic">He is persecuted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">v. 6</reference>); violent hands are laid upon him, and none hinders. It is the common fate of tyrants, when they fall into the power of their enemies, to be deserted by their flatterers, whom they took for their friends. We read of another enemy like this, of whom it is foretold that <hi type="italic">he shall come to his end and none shall help him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">Dan. xi. 45</reference>. Tiberius and Nero thus saw themselves abandoned. (3.) That he should be slain, and <hi type="italic">go down to the congregation of the dead,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">free among them, as the slain that are no more remembered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.88.5">Ps. lxxxviii. 5</reference>. He shall be <hi type="italic">weak as the dead</hi> are, and <hi type="italic">like unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10">v. 10</reference>. His <hi type="italic">pomp is brought down to the grave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">v. 11</reference>), that is, it perishes with him; the pomp of his life shall not, as usual, end in a funeral pomp. True glory (that is, true grace) will go up with the soul to heaven, but vain pomp will go down with the body to the grave: there is an end of it. <hi type="italic">The noise of his viols</hi> is now heard no more. Death is a farewell to the pleasures, as well as to the pomps, of this world. This mighty prince, that used to lie on a bed of down, to tread upon rich carpets, and to have coverings and canopies exquisitely fine, now shall have the <hi type="italic">worms spread under him and the worms covering him,</hi> worms bred out of his own putrefied body, which, though he fancied himself a god, proved him to be made of the same mould with other men. When we are pampering and decking our bodies it is good to remember they will be worms'-meat shortly. (4.) That he should not have the honour of a burial, much less of a decent one and in the sepulchres of his ancestors. <hi type="italic">The kings of the nations lie in glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.18">v. 18</reference>), either their dead bodies themselves so embalmed as to be preserved from putrefaction, as of old among the Egyptians, or their effigies (as with us) erected over their graves. Thus, as if they would defy the ignominy of death, they lay in a poor faint sort of glory, <hi type="italic">every one in his own house,</hi> that is, his own burying-place (for the grave is the house appointed for all living), a sleeping house, where the busy and troublesome will lie quiet and the troubled and weary lie at rest. But this king of Babylon is <hi type="italic">cast out</hi> and has no grave (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">v. 19</reference>); his dead body is thrown, like that of a beast, into the next ditch or upon the next dunghill, <hi type="italic">like an abominable branch</hi> of some noxious poisonous plant, which nobody will touch, or as the clothes of malefactors put to death and by the hand of justice <hi type="italic">thrust through with a sword,</hi> on whose dead bodies heaps of stones are raised, or they are thrown into some deep quarry among <hi type="italic">the stones of the pit.</hi> Nay, the king of Babylon's dead body shall be as the carcases of those who are slain in a battle, which are <hi type="italic">trodden under feet</hi> by the horses and soldiers and crushed to pieces. Thus he <hi type="italic">shall not be joined with his ancestors in burial,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.20">v. 20</reference>. To be denied decent burial is a disgrace, which, if it be inflicted for righteousness' sake (as <reference osisRef="Ps.79.2">Ps. lxxix. 2</reference>), may, as other similar reproaches, be rejoiced in (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">Matt. v. 12</reference>); it is the lot of the two witnesses, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.9">Rev. xi. 9</reference>. But if, as here, it be the just punishment of iniquity, it is an intimation that evil pursues impenitent sinners beyond death, greater evil than that, and that they shall <hi type="italic">rise to everlasting shame and contempt.</hi> <div eID="gen15802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15803" type="x-p"/> 4. The many triumphs that should be in his fall. <div eID="gen15803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15804" type="x-p"/> (1.) Those whom he had been a great tyrant and terror to will be glad that they are rid of him, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.7-Isa.14.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Now that he is gone <hi type="italic">the whole earth is at rest and is quiet,</hi> for he was the great disturber of the peace; now they all <hi type="italic">break forth into singing,</hi> for <hi type="italic">when the wicked perish there is shouting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.10">Prov. xi. 10</reference>); the fir-trees and cedars of Lebanon now think themselves safe; there is no danger now of their being cut down, to make way for his vast armies or to furnish him with timber. The neighbouring princes and great men, who are compared to fir-trees and cedars (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.2">Zech. xi. 2</reference>), may now be easy, and out of fear of being dispossessed of their rights, for <hi type="italic">the hammer of the whole earth is cut asunder and broken</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jer. l. 23</reference>), the axe that <hi type="italic">boasted itself against him that hewed with it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">ch. x. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen15804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15805" type="x-p"/> (2.) The congregation of the dead will bid him welcome to them, especially those whom he had barbarously hastened thither (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.9-Isa.14.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hell from beneath is moved for thee, to meet thee at thy coming,</hi> and to compliment thee upon thy arrival at their dark and dreadful regions." <hi type="italic">The chief ones of the earth,</hi> who when they were alive were kept in awe by him and durst not come near him, but rose from their thrones, to resign them to him, shall upbraid him with it when he comes into the state of the dead. They shall go forth to meet him, as they used to do when he made his public entry into cities he had become master of; with such a parade shall he be introduced into those regions of horror, to make his disgrace and torment the more grievous to him. They shall scoffingly rise from their thrones and seats there, and ask him if he will please to sit down in them, as he used to do in their thrones on earth? The confusion that will then cover him they shall make a jest of: "<hi type="italic">Hast thou also become weak as we?</hi> Who would have thought it? It is what thou thyself didst not expect it would ever come to when thou wast in every thing too hard for us. Thou that didst rank thyself among the immortal gods, art thou come to take thy fate among us poor mortal men? Where is thy pomp now, and where thy mirth? <hi type="italic">How hast thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer! son of the morning!</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11-Isa.14.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. The king of Babylon shone as brightly as the morning star, and fancied that wherever he came he brought day along with him; and has such an illustrious prince as this fallen, such a star become a clod of clay? Did ever any man fall from such a height of honour and power into such an abyss of shame and misery?" This has been commonly alluded to (and it is a mere allusion) to illustrate the fall of the angels, who were as morning stars (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 7</reference>), but <hi type="italic">how have they fallen! How art thou cut down to the ground,</hi> and levelled with it, that <hi type="italic">didst weaken the nations!</hi> God will reckon with those that invade the rights and disturb the peace of mankind, for he is King of nations as well as of saints. Now this reception of the king of Babylon into the regions of the dead, which is here described, surely is something more than a flight of fancy, and is designed to teach these solid truths:—[1.] That there is an invisible world, a world of spirits, to which the souls of men remove at death and in which they exist and act in a state of separation from the body. [2.] That separate souls have acquaintance and converse with each other, though we have none with them: the parable of the rich man and Lazarus intimates this. [3.] That death and hell will be death and hell indeed to those that fall unsanctified from the height of this world's pomps and the fulness of its pleasures. <hi type="italic">Son, remember,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen15805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15806" type="x-p"/> (3.) Spectators will stand amazed at his fall. When he shall be <hi type="italic">brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit,</hi> and be lodged there, <hi type="italic">those that see him shall narrowly look upon him, and consider him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.15-Isa.14.16">v. 15, 16</reference>); they shall scarcely believe their own eyes. "Never was death so great a change to any man as it is to him. Is it possible that a man, who a few hours ago looked so great, so pleasant, and was so splendidly adorned and attended, should now look so ghastly, so despicable, and lie thus naked and neglected? <hi type="italic">Is this the man that made the earth to tremble and shook kingdoms?</hi> Who could have thought he should ever come to this?" <reference osisRef="Ps.82.7">Ps. lxxxii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen15806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15807" type="x-p"/> 5. Here is an inference drawn from all this (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The seed of evil-doers shall never be renowned.</hi> The princes of the Babylonian monarchy were all a seed of evil-doers, oppressors of the people of God, and therefore they had this infamy entailed upon them. <hi type="italic">They shall not be renowned for ever</hi> (so some read it); they may look big for a time, but all their pomp will only render their disgrace at last the more shameful. There is no credit in a sinful way. <div eID="gen15807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15808" type="x-p"/> II. The utter ruin of the royal family is here foretold, together with the desolation of The royal city. <div eID="gen15808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15809" type="x-p"/> 1. The royal family is to be wholly extirpated. The Medes and Persians, that are to be employed in this destroying work, are ordered, when they have slain Belshazzar, to <hi type="italic">prepare slaughter for his children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.21">v. 21</reference>) and not to spare them. The little ones of Babylon must be <hi type="italic">dashed against the stones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.137.9">Ps. cxxxvii. 9</reference>. These orders sound very harshly; but, (1.) They must suffer <hi type="italic">for the iniquity of their fathers,</hi> which is often <hi type="italic">visited upon the children,</hi> to show how much God hates sin and is displeased at it, and to deter sinners from it, which is the end of punishment. Nebuchadnezzar had slain Zedekiah's sons (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jer. lii. 10</reference>), and, for that iniquity of his, his seed are paid in the same coin. (2.) They must be cut off now, that they <hi type="italic">may not rise up to possess the land</hi> and do as much mischief in their day as their fathers had done in theirs—that they may not be as vexatious to the world by building cities for the support of their tyranny (which was Nimrod's policy, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10-Gen.10.11">Gen. x. 10, 11</reference>) as their ancestors had been by destroying cities. Pharaoh oppressed Israel in Egypt by setting them to build cities, <reference osisRef="Exod.1.11">Exod. i. 11</reference>. The providence of God consults the welfare of nations more than we are aware of by cutting off some who, if they had lived, would have done mischief. Justly may the enemies cut off the children: <hi type="italic">For I will rise up against them, saith the Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.22">v. 22</reference>), and if God reveal it as his mind that he will have it done, as none can hinder it, so none need scruple to further it. Babylon perhaps was proud of the numbers of her royal family, but God had determined to <hi type="italic">cut off the name and remnant</hi> of it, so that none should be left, to have both the sons and grandsons of the king slain; and yet we are sure he never did, nor ever will do, any wrong to any of his creatures. <div eID="gen15809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15810" type="x-p"/> 2. The royal city is to be demolished and deserted, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.23">v. 23</reference>. It shall be a possession for solitary frightful birds, particularly <hi type="italic">the bittern,</hi> joined with the cormorant and the owl, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.11">ch. xxiv. 11</reference>. And thus the utter destruction of the New-Testament Babylon is illustrated, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev. xviii. 2</reference>. It <hi type="italic">has become a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.</hi> Babylon lay low, so that when it was deserted, and no care taken to drain the land, it soon became <hi type="italic">pools of water,</hi> standing noisome puddles, as unhealthful as they were unpleasant: and thus God <hi type="italic">will sweep it with the besom of destruction.</hi> When a people have nothing among them but dirt and filth, and will not be made clean with the besom of reformation, what can they expect but to be swept off the face of the earth with the besom of destruction?
entries.4851537399cefd087869f88f3ef780b8c63625c8: <div eID="gen15810" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of the Assyrians; The Doom of the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen15811" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall it stand: <hi type="super">25</hi> That I will break the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains tread him under foot: then shall his yoke depart from off them, and his burden depart from off their shoulders. <hi type="super">26</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the purpose that is purposed upon the whole earth: and this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the hand that is stretched out upon all the nations. <hi type="super">27</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul <hi type="italic">it?</hi> and his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out, and who shall turn it back? <hi type="super">28</hi> In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden. <hi type="super">29</hi> Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a fiery flying serpent. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the needy shall lie down in safety: and I will kill thy root with famine, and he shall slay thy remnant. <hi type="super">31</hi> Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, <hi type="italic">art</hi> dissolved: for there shall come from the north a smoke, and none <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> alone in his appointed times. <hi type="super">32</hi> What shall <hi type="italic">one</hi> then answer the messengers of the nation? That the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it. <div eID="gen15811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15812" type="x-p"/> The destruction of Babylon and the Chaldean empire was a thing at a great distance; the empire had not risen to any considerable height when its fall was here foretold: it was almost 200 years from this prediction of Babylon's fall to the accomplishment of it. Now the people to whom Isaiah prophesied might ask, "What is this to us, or what shall we be the better for it, and what assurance shall we have of it?" To both questions he answers in these verses, by a prediction of the ruin both of the Assyrians and of the Philistines, the present enemies that infested them, which they should shortly be eye-witnesses of and have benefit by. These would be a present comfort to them, and a pledge of future deliverance, for the confirming of the faith of their posterity. God is to his people the same to day that he was yesterday and will be hereafter; and he will for ever be the same that he has been and is. Here is, <div eID="gen15812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15813" type="x-p"/> I. Assurance given of the destruction of the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will break the Assyrian in my land.</hi> Sennacherib brought a very formidable army into the land of Judah, but there God broke it, broke all his regiments by the sword of a destroying angel. Note, Those who wrongfully invade God's land shall find that it is at their peril: and those who with unhallowed feet trample upon his holy mountains shall themselves there be trodden under foot. God undertakes to do this himself, his people having no might against the great company that came against them: "<hi type="italic">I will break the Assyrian;</hi> let me alone to do it who have angels, hosts of angels, at command." Now the breaking of the power of the Assyrian would be the breaking of the yoke from off the neck of God's people: <hi type="italic">His burden shall depart from off their shoulders,</hi> the burden of quartering that vast army and paying contribution; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the Assyrian must be broken, that Judah and Jerusalem may be eased. Let those that make themselves a yoke and a burden to God's people see what they are to expect. Now, 1. This prophecy is here ratified and confirmed by an oath (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts hath sworn,</hi> that he might show the immutability of his counsel, and that his people may have strong consolation, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. What is here said of this particular intention is true of all God's purposes: <hi type="italic">As I have thought, so shall it come to pass;</hi> for <hi type="italic">he is in one mind, and who can turn him?</hi> Nor is he ever put upon new counsels, or obliged to take new measures, as men often are when things occur which they did not foresee. Let those who are <hi type="italic">the called according to God's purpose</hi> comfort themselves with this, that, <hi type="italic">as God has purposed, so shall it stand,</hi> and on that their stability depends. 2. The breaking of the Assyrian power is made a specimen of what God would do with all the powers of the nations that were engaged against him and his church (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the purpose that is purposed upon the whole earth</hi> (<hi type="italic">the whole world,</hi> so the LXX.), <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants of the earth</hi> (so the Chaldee), not only upon the Assyrian empire (which was then reckoned to be in a manner all the world, as afterwards the Roman empire was, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Luke ii. 1</reference>, and with it many nations fell that had dependence upon it), but upon all those states and potentates that should at any time attack his land, his mountains. The fate of the Assyrian shall be theirs; they shall soon find that they meddle to their own hurt. Jerusalem, as it was to the Assyrians, will be <hi type="italic">to all people a burdensome stone; all that burden themselves with it shall infallibly be cut to pieces by it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zech. xii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">6</reference>. The same hand of power and justice that is now to be stretched out against the Assyrian for invading the people of God shall be <hi type="italic">stretched out upon all the nations</hi> that do likewise. It is still true, and will ever be so, <hi type="italic">Cursed is he that curses God's Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.9">Num. xxiv. 9</reference>. God will be an enemy to his people's enemies, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.22">Exod. xxiii. 22</reference>. 3. All the powers on earth are defied to change God's counsel (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts has purposed</hi> to break the Assyrian's yoke, and every rod of the wicked laid upon the lot of the righteous; <hi type="italic">and who shall disannul this purpose?</hi> Who can persuade him to recall it, or find out a plea to evade it? <hi type="italic">His hand is stretched out</hi> to execute this purpose; <hi type="italic">and who has power</hi> enough <hi type="italic">to turn it back</hi> or to stay the course of his judgments?" <div eID="gen15813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15814" type="x-p"/> II. Assurance is likewise given of the destruction of the Philistines and their power. This burden, this prophecy, that lay as a load upon them, to sink their state, came <hi type="italic">in the year that king Ahaz died,</hi> which was the first year of Hezekiah's reign, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.28">v. 28</reference>. When a good king came in the room of a bad one then this acceptable message was sent among them. When we reform, then, and not till then, we may look for good news from heaven. Now here we have, 1. A rebuke to the Philistines for triumphing in the death of king Uzziah. He had been as a serpent to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.29">v. 29</reference>), had bitten them, had smitten them, had brought them very low, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2 Chron. xxvi. 6</reference>. He <hi type="italic">warred against the Philistines, broke down their walls, and built cities among them.</hi> But when Uzziah died, or rather abdicated, it was told with joy in Gath and <hi type="italic">published in the streets of Ashkelon.</hi> It is inhuman thus to rejoice in our neighbour's fall. But let them not be secure; for though when Uzziah was dead they made reprisals upon Ahaz, and took many of the cities of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2 Chron. xxviii. 18</reference>), yet <hi type="italic">out of the root</hi> of Uzziah <hi type="italic">should come a cockatrice,</hi> a more formidable enemy than Uzziah was, even Hezekiah, the fruit of whose government should be to them <hi type="italic">a fiery flying serpent,</hi> for he should fall upon them with incredible swiftness and fury: we find he did so. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.8">2 Kings xviii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">He smote the Philistines even to Gaza.</hi> Note, If God remove one useful instrument in the midst of his usefulness, he can, and will, raise up others to carry on and complete the same work that they were employed in and left unfinished. 2. A prophecy of the destruction of the Philistines by famine and war. (1.) By famine, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.30">v. 30</reference>. "When the people of God, whom the Philistines has wasted, and distressed, and impoverished, shall enjoy plenty again," and <hi type="italic">the first-born of their poor shall feed</hi> (the poorest among them shall have food convenient), then, as for the Philistines, God will kill <hi type="italic">their root with famine.</hi> That which was their strength, and with which they thought themselves established as the tree is by the root, shall be starved and dried up by degrees, as those die that die by famine; and thus <hi type="italic">he shall slay the remnant:</hi> those that escape from one destruction are but reserved for another; and, when there are but a few left, those few shall at length be cut off, for God will make a full end. (2.) By war. When <hi type="italic">the needy</hi> of God's people <hi type="italic">shall lie down in safety,</hi> not terrified with the alarms of war, but delighting in the songs of peace, then every gate and every city of the Philistines shall be howling and crying (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">v. 31</reference>), and there shall be a total dissolution of their state; for from Judea, which lay north of the Philistines, <hi type="italic">there shall come a smoke</hi> (a vast army raising a great dust, a smoke that shall be the indication of a devouring fire at hand), <hi type="italic">and none</hi> of all that army <hi type="italic">shall be alone in his appointed times;</hi> none shall straggle or be missing when they are to engage; but they shall all be vigorous and unanimous in attacking the common enemy, when the time appointed for the doing of it comes. None of them shall decline the public service, as, in Deborah's time, Reuben abode among the sheepfolds and Asher on the sea-shore, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.16-Judg.5.17">Judg. v. 16, 17</reference>. When God has work to do he will wonderfully endow and dispose men for it. <div eID="gen15814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15815" type="x-p"/> III. The good use that should be made of all these events for the encouragement of the people of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">What shall one then answer the messengers of the nations?</hi> <div eID="gen15815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15816" type="x-p"/> 1. This implies, (1.) That the great things God does for his people are, and cannot but be, taken notice of by their neighbours; those among the heathen make remarks upon them, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.2">Ps. cxxvi. 2</reference>. (2.) That messengers will be sent to enquire concerning them. Jacob and Israel had long been a people distinguished from all others and dignified with uncommon favours; and therefore some for good-will, others for ill-will, and all for curiosity, are inquisitive concerning them. (3.) That it concerns us always to be ready to give a reason of the hope that we have in the providence of God, as well as in his grace, in answer to every one that asks it, <hi type="italic">with meekness and fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>. And we need go no further than the sacred truths of God's word for a reason; for God, in all he does, is fulfilling the scripture. (4.) The issue of God's dealings with his people shall be so clearly and manifestly glorious that any one, every one, shall be able to give an account of them to those that enquire concerning them. Now, <div eID="gen15816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15817" type="x-p"/> 2. The answer which is to be given to the messengers of the nations is, (1.) That God is and will be a faithful friend to his church and people, and will secure and advance their interests. Tell them that <hi type="italic">the Lord has founded Zion.</hi> This gives an account both of the work itself that is done and of the reason of it. What is God doing in the world, and what is he designing in all the revolutions of states and kingdoms, in the ruin of some nations and the rise of others? He is, in all this, founding Zion; he is aiming at the advancement of his church's interests; and what he aims at he will accomplish. The messengers of the nations, when they sent to enquire concerning Hezekiah's successes against the Philistines, expected to learn by what politics, counsels, and arts of war he carried his point; but they are told that these successes were not owing to any thing of that nature, but to the care God took of his church and the interest he had in it. The Lord has founded Zion, and therefore the Philistines must fall. (2.) That his church has and will have a dependence upon him: <hi type="italic">The poor of his people shall trust in it,</hi> his poor people who have lately been brought very low, even the poorest of them; they more than others, for they have nothing else to trust to, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.12-Zeph.3.13">Zeph. iii. 12, 13</reference>. The <hi type="italic">poor receive the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Matt. xi. 5</reference>. They shall trust to this, to this great truth, that the Lord has founded Zion; on this they shall build their hopes, and not on an arm of flesh. This ought to give us abundant satisfaction as to public affairs, that however it may go with particular persons, parties, and interests, the church, having God himself for its founder and Christ the rock for its foundation, cannot but stand firm. <hi type="italic">The poor of his people shall betake themselves to it</hi> (so some read it), shall join themselves to his church and embark in its interests; they shall concur with God in his designs to establish his people, and shall wind up all on the same plan, and make all their little concerns and projects bend to that. Those that take God's people for their people must be willing to take their lot with them and cast in their lot among them. Let the messengers of the nations know that the poor Israelites, who trust in God, having, like Zion, their foundation in the holy mountains (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.1">Ps. lxxxvii. 1</reference>), are like Zion, which <hi type="italic">cannot be removed, but abides for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">Ps. cxxv. 1</reference>), and therefore they will not fear what man can do unto them.  <chapter eID="Isa.14"/> <div eID="gen15817" type="x-p"/>

The Certainty of Deliverance from Babylon.</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.4-Isa.14.23">Is 14:4-23</reference>. The Jews' Triumphal Song Thereat.</title> <div sID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> "It moves in lengthened elegiac measure like a song of lamentation for the dead, and is full of lofty scorn" [Herder].<div eID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27">Is 14:24-27</reference>. Confirmation of This by the Hereforetold Destruction of the Assyrians under Sennacherib;</title> <div sID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> a pledge to assure the captives in Babylon that He who, with such ease, overthrew the Assyrian, could likewise effect His purpose as to Babylon. The Babylonian king, the subject of this prediction, is Belshazzar, as representative of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>).<div eID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8570"/><hi type="bold">1. choose--</hi>"set His choice upon." A deliberate predilection [Horsley]. Their restoration is grounded on their election (see <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.22">Psa 102:13-22</reference>).<div eID="gen14012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>proselytes (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Es 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.10">Ac 2:10</reference>; 17:4, 17). Tacitus, a heathen [Histories, 5.5], attests the fact of numbers of the Gentiles having become Jews in his time. An earnest of the future effect on the heathen world of the Jews' spiritual restoration (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Is 60:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">5, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14013" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9608905449173fd022a23322690063234abaaae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8571"/><div sID="gen14014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8571"/><hi type="bold">2. the people--</hi>of Babylon, primarily. Of the whole Gentile world ultimately (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Is 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.20">66:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">60:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their place--</hi>Judea (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.6">Ezr 1:1-6</reference>).<div eID="gen14015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">possess--</hi>receive in possession.<div eID="gen14016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">captives--</hi>not by physical, but by moral might; the force of love, and regard to Israel's God (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.14">Is 60:14</reference>). <div eID="gen14017" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc3bf91c0ae35caf187c27956e68468407d766b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8572"/><div sID="gen14018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8572"/><hi type="bold">3. rest--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Is 28:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.25">Eze 28:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen14018" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.4-Isa.14.8">Is 14:4-8</reference>. A Chorus of Jews Express Their Joyful Surprise at Babylon's Downfall.</title> <div sID="gen14019" type="x-p"/> The whole earth rejoices; the cedars of Lebanon taunt him. <div eID="gen14019" type="x-p"/>
entries.7afc3fbf867784ed2cba1c22c9f772fd2d760c20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8573"/><div sID="gen14020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8573"/><hi type="bold">4. proverb--</hi>The Orientals, having few books, embodied their thoughts in weighty, figurative, briefly expressed gnomes. Here a taunting song of triumph (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king--</hi>the ideal representative of Babylon; perhaps Belshazzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>). The mystical Babylon is ultimately meant.<div eID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">golden city--</hi>rather, "the exactress of gold" [Maurer]. But the old translators read differently in the Hebrew, "oppression," which the parallelism favors (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Is 3:5</reference>). <div eID="gen14022" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5ee0a5814862bb0c70cf51fcb3b1347e0ec92a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8574"/><div sID="gen14023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8574"/><hi type="bold">5. staff--</hi>not the scepter (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>), but the staff with which one strikes others, as he is speaking of more tyrants than one (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.29">14:29</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rulers--</hi>tyrants, as the parallelism "the wicked" proves (compare see on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Is 13:2</reference>). <div eID="gen14024" type="x-p"/>
entries.b459416ec3695c798d987ceea5a171928dcdbf1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8575"/><div sID="gen14025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8575"/><hi type="bold">6. people--</hi>the peoples subjected to Babylon.<div eID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is persecuted--</hi>the Hebrew is rather, active, "which persecuted them, without any to hinder him" [Vulgate, Jerome, and Horsley]. <div eID="gen14026" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a4072dfb21971bb37067e3ccd7aaf88129af67f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8576"/><div sID="gen14027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8576"/><hi type="bold">7. they--</hi>the once subject nations of the whole earth. Houbigant places the stop after "fir trees" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.8">Is 14:8</reference>), "The very fir trees break forth," &c. But the parallelism is better in English Version. <div eID="gen14027" type="x-p"/>
entries.613a7f34e194a59b7a8f6ce2d88d99a4895cb44f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8577"/><div sID="gen14028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8577"/><hi type="bold">8. the fir trees--</hi>now left undisturbed. Probably a kind of evergreen.<div eID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice at thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.96.12">Psa 96:12</reference>). At thy fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen14029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no feller--</hi>as formerly, when thou wast in power (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Is 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">37:24</reference>).<div eID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.9-Isa.14.11">Is 14:9-11</reference>. The Scene Changes from Earth to Hell.</title> <div sID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> Hades (the Amenthes of Egypt), the unseen abode of the departed; some of its tenants, once mighty monarchs, are represented by a bold personification as rising from their seats in astonishment at the descent among them of the humbled king of Babylon. This proves, in opposition to Warburton [The Divine Legation], that the belief existed among the Jews that there was a Sheol or Hades, in which the "Rephaim" or manes of the departed abode. <div eID="gen14031" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef2b226c68e55a5458681fe8d95309acb97ce287: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8578"/><div sID="gen14032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8578"/><hi type="bold">9. moved--</hi>put into agitation.<div eID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thee--</hi>that is, "at thee"; towards thee; explained by "to meet thee at thy coming" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief ones--</hi>literally, "goats"; so rams, leaders of the flock; princes (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>). The idea of wickedness on a gigantic scale is included (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Eze 34:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">Mt 25:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">33</reference>). Magee derives "Rephaim" (English Version, "the dead") from a Hebrew root, "to resolve into first elements"; so "the deceased" (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Is 26:14</reference>) "ghosts" (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.16">Pr 21:16</reference>). These being magnified by the imagination of the living into gigantic stature, gave their name to giants in general (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Ge 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.18">Eze 32:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">21</reference>). "Rephaim," translated in the Septuagint, "giants" (compare see on <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job 26:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">6</reference>). Thence, as the giant Rephaim of Canaan were notorious even in that guilty land, enormous wickedness became connected with the term. So the Rephaim came to be the wicked spirits in Gehenna, the lower of the two portions into which Sheol is divided. <div eID="gen14034" type="x-p"/>
entries.da95ce73d6a6fd2b8f68ba10a2dc9d04e1ec6759: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8579"/><div sID="gen14035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8579"/>10. They taunt him and derive from his calamity consolation under their own (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference>).<div eID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weak--</hi>as a shade bereft of blood and life. Rephaim, "the dead," may come from a Hebrew root, meaning similarly "feeble," "powerless." The speech of the departed closes with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>. <div eID="gen14036" type="x-p"/>
entries.b66bc0d4d3ea60cc894547eb0afad7c835f3f922: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8580"/><div sID="gen14037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8580"/>11. "Pomp" and music, the accompaniment of Babylon's former feastings (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Is 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.8">24:8</reference>), give place to the corruption and the stillness of the grave (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Eze 32:27</reference>).<div eID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worm--</hi>that is bred in putridity.<div eID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worms--</hi>properly those from which the crimson dye is obtained. Appropriate here; instead of the crimson coverlet, over thee shall be "worms." Instead of the gorgeous couch, "under thee" shall be the maggot.<div eID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.12-Isa.14.15">Is 14:12-15</reference>. The Jews Address Him Again as a Fallen Once-bright Star.</title> <div sID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> The language is so framed as to apply to the Babylonian king primarily, and at the same time to shadow forth through him, the great final enemy, the man of sin, Antichrist, of Daniel, St. Paul, and St. John; he alone shall fulfil exhaustively all the lineaments here given. <div eID="gen14040" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ca4d312d50c72cdbcb60441ecb2258508f899f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8581"/><div sID="gen14041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8581"/><hi type="bold">12. Lucifer--</hi>"day star." A title truly belonging to Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Re 22:16</reference>), "the bright and morning star," and therefore hereafter to be assumed by Antichrist. Gesenius, however, renders the Hebrew here as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.12">Eze 21:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.11.2">Zec 11:2</reference>, "howl."<div eID="gen14041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weaken--</hi>"prostrate"; as in <reference osisRef="Exod.17.13">Ex 17:13</reference>, "discomfit." <div eID="gen14042" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee0f7bd3bbff0d510054eead4801ba004998375a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8582"/><div sID="gen14043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8582"/><hi type="bold">13. above ... God--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Da 8:10</reference>, "stars" express earthly potentates. "The stars" are often also used to express heavenly principalities (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job 38:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mount of the congregation--</hi>the place of solemn meeting between God and His people in the temple at Jerusalem. In <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">Da 11:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>, this is attributed to Antichrist.<div eID="gen14044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sides of the north--</hi>namely, the sides of Mount Moriah on which the temple was built; north of Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>). However, the parallelism supports the notion that the Babylonian king expresses himself according to his own, and not Jewish opinions (so in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">Is 10:10</reference>) thus "mount of the congregation" will mean the northern mountain (perhaps in Armenia) fabled by the Babylonians to be the common meeting-place of their gods. "Both sides" imply the angle in which the sides meet; and so the expression comes to mean "the extreme parts of the north." So the Hindus place the Meru, the dwelling-place of their gods, in the north, in the Himalayan mountains. So the Greeks, in the northern Olympus. The Persian followers of Zoroaster put the Ai-bordsch in the Caucasus north of them. The allusion to the stars harmonizes with this; namely, that those near the North Pole, the region of the aurora borealis (compare see on <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference>) [Maurer, Septuagint, Syriac]. <div eID="gen14045" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb49ab8490224ad96afc142dff5dba9c8a9d4524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8583"/><div sID="gen14046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8583"/><hi type="bold">14. clouds--</hi>rather, "the cloud," singular. Perhaps there is a reference to the cloud, the symbol of the divine presence (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Ex 13:21</reference>). So this tallies with <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>, "above all that is called God"; as here "above ... the cloud"; and as the Shekinah-cloud was connected with the temple, there follows, "he as God sitteth in the temple of God," answering to "I will be like the Most High" here. Moreover, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.4">Re 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.5">5</reference>, represents Antichrist as seated in Babylon, to which city, literal and spiritual, Isaiah refers here. <div eID="gen14046" type="x-p"/>
entries.a103202d74a60683382c531803eafa011a847079: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8584"/><div sID="gen14047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8584"/><hi type="bold">15. to hell--</hi>to Sheol (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">Is 14:6</reference>), thou who hast said, "I will ascend into heaven" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.23">Mt 11:23</reference>).<div eID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sides of the pit--</hi>antithetical to the "sides of the north" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>). Thus the reference is to the sides of the sepulcher round which the dead were arranged in niches. But Maurer here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>, translates, "the extreme," or innermost parts of the sepulchre: as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.23">Eze 32:23</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">1Sa 24:3</reference>). <div eID="gen14048" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6fb225124ad81a42fee4ff24e3f2609734c1b34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8585"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.16-Isa.14.20">Is 14:16-20</reference>. The Passers-by Contemplate with Astonishment the Body of the King of Babylon Cast Out, Instead of Lying in a Splendid Mausoleum, and Can Hardly Believe Their Senses that It Is He.</title> <div sID="gen14049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8585"/><hi type="bold">16. narrowly look--</hi>to be certain they are not mistaken.<div eID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consider--</hi>"meditate upon" [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14050" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cdce9a5a782fc188fa5288c758bb9396f721670: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8586"/><div sID="gen14051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8586"/><hi type="bold">17. opened not ... house ... prisoners--</hi>But Maurer, as Margin, "Did not let his captives loose homewards." <div eID="gen14051" type="x-p"/>
entries.2060d45030b577a51a7cc16db6f628b829efa022: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8587"/><div sID="gen14052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8587"/><hi type="bold">18. All--</hi>that is, This is the usual practice.<div eID="gen14052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in glory--</hi>in a grand mausoleum.<div eID="gen14053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house--</hi>that is, "sepulchre," as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.5">Ec 12:5</reference>; "grave" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Is 14:19</reference>). To be excluded from the family sepulcher was a mark of infamy (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.3">Is 34:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jr 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.22">1Ki 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.20">2Ch 21:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.25">24:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.27">28:27</reference>). <div eID="gen14054" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f65b5675ae592ae0e19a5bfcdb462eb47e785e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8588"/><div sID="gen14055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8588"/><hi type="bold">19. cast out of--</hi>not that he had lain in the grave and was then cast out of it, but "cast out without a grave," such as might have been expected by thee ("thy").<div eID="gen14055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch--</hi>a useless sucker starting up from the root of a tree, and cut away by the husbandman.<div eID="gen14056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raiment of those ... slain--</hi>covered with gore, and regarded with abhorrence as unclean by the Jews. Rather, "clothed (that is, covered) with the slain"; as in <reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>, "My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thrust through--</hi>that is, "the slain who have been thrust through," &c.<div eID="gen14058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stones of ... pit--</hi>whose bodies are buried in sepulchres excavated amidst stones, whereas the king of Babylon is an unburied "carcass trodden under foot." <div eID="gen14059" type="x-p"/>
entries.7fd52450973fe7d6245cfa92b7fd42e7a806170c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8589"/><div sID="gen14060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8589"/><hi type="bold">20. not ... joined with them--</hi>whereas the princes slain with thee shall be buried, thou shalt not.<div eID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... destroyed ... land--</hi>Belshazzar (or Naboned) oppressed his land with wars and tyranny, so that he was much hated [Xenophon, Cyropædia 4.6, 3; 7.5, 32].<div eID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seed ... never be renowned--</hi>rather, "shall not be named for ever"; the Babylonian dynasty shall end with Belshazzar; his family shall not be perpetuated [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14062" type="x-p"/>
entries.4edb8ed650aae2f6b462353a3a4d0301326b04be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8590"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.21-Isa.14.23">Is 14:21-23</reference>. God's Determination to Destroy Babylon.</title> <div sID="gen14063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8590"/><hi type="bold">21. Prepare, &c.--</hi>charge to the Medes and Persians, as if they were God's conscious instruments.<div eID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his children--</hi>Belshazzar's (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rise--</hi>to occupy the places of their fathers.<div eID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill ... with cities--</hi>Maurer translates, "enemies," as the Hebrew means in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">1Sa 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference>; namely, lest they inundate the world with their armies. Vitringa translates, "disturbers." In English Version the meaning is, "lest they fill the land with such cities" of pride as Babylon was. <div eID="gen14066" type="x-p"/>
entries.a09b5c82a5268506d81b08aaa4f14cf41edee094: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8591"/><div sID="gen14067" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8591"/><hi type="bold">22. against them--</hi>the family of the king of Babylon.<div eID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name--</hi>all the male representatives, so that the name shall become extinct (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.5">Is 56:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.5">Ru 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant--</hi>all that is left of them. The dynasty shall cease (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.28-Dan.5.31">Da 5:28-31</reference>). Compare as to Babylon in general, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.62">Jr 51:62</reference>. <div eID="gen14069" type="x-p"/>
entries.daefcad42ef4251316133af36c2878a75b97b80e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8592"/><div sID="gen14070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8592"/><hi type="bold">23. bittern--</hi>rather, "the hedgehog" [Maurer and Gesenius]. Strabo (16:1) states that enormous hedgehogs were found in the islands of the Euphrates.<div eID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pools--</hi>owing to Cyrus turning the waters of the Euphrates over the country.<div eID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">besom--</hi>sweep-net [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.10">1Ki 14:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Ki 21:13</reference>).<div eID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27">Is 14:24-27</reference>.
